Our goal is to utilize external knowledge to enhance the process of answering questions within the ASQA framework. To achieve this, we incorporate JSON-based external knowledge that is relevant to each question. As opposed to existing methods which rely on symbolic methods requiring a significant manual effort to define and update, we propose a fully automatic approach based on semantic relations. Our framework consists of three main steps: first we select a subset of knowledge from a large knowledge base, then we fine-tune the model using this selected data, finally we evaluate our approach and demonstrate its superiority over the baseline method based on automatic and human assessments.

Recent astronomical observations in the infrared and visible light spectra require accurate small-cation spectral models to be created. However, due to multiple and complicated electron transitions, this is challenging for cations that contain elements beyond hydrogen, helium, and sodium. This paper aims to fill that gap by providing an extensive spectral model for the $\text{MgH}^+$ cation to the 12,000 cm$^{-1}$ range, which includes a comprehensive construction of its electronic structure, detailed description of its dynamic properties, and a comprehensive discussion of its photon interaction based on a constructed comprehensive system basis set. This system basis set was established through the combination of precise cation basis set, magnetic vector potentials derived from the Lehach-Powell method, and a specialized electronic state classification system. With the use of the constructed tools, the full spectral range of the $\text{MgH}^+$ cation was covered, which allowed for its identification in various astronomical environments and confirmed its presence in space.

A significant issue with training machine learning models on distributed data is the extensive communication required for model updates during gradient descent. To address this problem, novel approaches like using sparse approximations of sparse gradients have shown great potential. Building on this idea, we introduce the random walk approach (RWA) for calculating sparse gradients in the calculation of sparse gradients used in model training. We demonstrate that our approach effectively reduces the after-strong-convexity optimality gap and requires only a single multiplication with the matrix $Q$ per iteration, offering an efficient implementation suitable for distributed systems. Our theoretical and empirical analyses highlight the effectiveness of the random walk approach compared to previous methods, providing a more practical and efficient alternative for estimating sparse gradients.

A significant increase in crimes committed by nonviolent offenders in the 1990s in Ohio led to new legislation mandating that convicted individuals undergo evaluation and potential mental health treatment post-sentencing. A dataset of 9,448 offenders from the 2010 to 2014 period was analyzed, comparing those who received court-ordered treatment with those who did not, to assess the impact of treatment on reoffending within two years. Results showed a 13 percent lower reoffending rate for those who received treatment, with variations in estimates depending on the type of crime committed. There was a lower reoffending rate found for property-related crimes and drug offenses among offenders who received treatment, with reductions of approximately 24 percent and 19 percent, respectively. There was no significant difference in violent or personal crime recidivism rates. Additional analysis into length of time until reoffending and sex-specific effects of treatment were also conducted.

Understanding the microstructure of materials is crucial to predicting their properties, and materials with complex and diverse atomic arrangements require efficient analysis tools. Graph neural networks (GNNs) have been used in materials science to model structural properties and chemical reactivity, and we have developed a framework called G2Point to automate local atomic configuration modeling and generate reliable GNN training data in large quantities. This framework ensures high-quality GNN representations by designing a series of graph augmentation and message-passing steps, and we have demonstrated its effectiveness in generating high-fidelity GNN data and improving the accuracy of global model training, yielding gains of up to 9% gain in modeling Gaussian processes and 5% in training neural networks.

If a sequence of random variables in a metric space converges weakly to a distribution, then for any continuous function of interest, the estimate can also converge weakly to its corresponding function of the parameter under certain conditions. This concept is widely utilized in statistics to enhance hypothesis testing and to develop efficient algorithms for estimating parameters. This paper explores these applications in specific settings, including the estimation of the mean of a random variable, the median of a random variable, and even more complex scenarios such as support vectors, extreme values, and quantiles, all while considering both discrete and continuous cases.

Deep learning models for knowledge tracing have been examined by various studies with conclusive results, yet comparing these models is often problematic due to the lack of agreement on reimplementation details and the high computational cost of experiments. We experience a need for accurate, efficient, and transparent benchmarking of knowledge tracing methods and identify existing benchmarks as falling short of this goal. Existing benchmarks involve excessive computational costs for frequent reruns with new datasets, leading to model comparison results that are unreliable due to inadequate seed management. We have developed a new benchmark named ADAPT Bench, which features 100-hour model training on a single GPU, ensures transparent results, and provides an entry-level cost of approximately $200 for model comparison studies. Our benchmark incorporates seed management into the training process, with seed settings openly documented. We have reimplemented multiple models including FAIT, RAKT, AT, and AT's teacher student stages, using existing public codebases. The results show that our results can be obtained with a minimal computational cost, and are openly available for research purposes at the URL https://zhengqiank/ADAPTBench/.

Given a metric space $X$, we introduce and examine the properties of the operator $\mathcal{M}$, which maps the set of all closed convex functions on $X$ to its subset consisting of functions that are solutions to a specific type of equation. For any two convex functions, there is a unique solution between them in the sense of an intermediate value. This solution can be characterized using the operator $\mathcal{M}$, which is shown to be both closed and strongly overjective when associated with a class of partial differential equations.

The veriT proof format, introduced in 2014 at the PxTP workshop, has seen continuous development and now supports SMT-LIB 2.0, including arrays, integers, and reals, as well as lemmas and axioms. This format has also been enhanced to support explanations for refutations and is widely used in competitions for PxTP and SMT-C unclamped proofs. We have updated the format to accommodate external proofs and can integrate with existing PxTP tools through a simple parser. This integration enables combining results from different solvers and can be applied in scenarios like merging results from different solvers and verifying complex proofs with the help of PxTP tools. We have demonstrated this by connecting the best entries from the SMT-C unclamped competitions with each other and with the veriT solver. This combined approach has achieved top-3 results in the recent SMT-C unclamped competitions. We have made our improvements and tools available and encourage the community to use and contribute to them. This will help in continuing the format's development and in achieving even better results in future competitions.

A new strategy called FedBuff is proposed to address scalability and data privacy concerns in large-scale federated learning. In FedBuff, selected participants store their updated model parameters locally, rather than submitting them to the server during each iteration. This reduces communication overhead and prevents other participants from learning about the updated parameters, thereby preserving data privacy. For selected participants, the communication cost is lowered, and our analysis shows that FedBuff outperforms traditional methods. Furthermore, the FedBuff algorithm can achieve accurate aggregation with minimal overhead and is capable of handling large-scale systems. Experimental results on large datasets like CIFAR-100 and ImageNet demonstrate that FedBuff achieves accuracy on par with centralized training, even in large-scale settings.

The use of transfer learning in speech recognition has been expanding rapidly, primarily due to the massive amount of unlabeled data that can be processed using self-supervised methods. Although early studies focused on audio processing in general, recent advancements have significantly boosted performance in specific speech recognition tasks. While primarily evaluated as unidirectional transfers from a source language to a target language, the feasibility of bidirectional transfers was initially investigated. Recent studies utilizing state-of-the-art encoder models have shown transfer learning's potential when similarity between languages is low, and have improved upon baseline systems using UNSD and FSD500 datasets. To build on these findings, our work utilizes a simpler yet widely adopted transfer learning framework, based on linear projection of latent features. Our results show that basic setup is sufficiently effective, and allows for comparable source and target languages during the training process. To further demonstrate our approach, we provide several examples of speech synthesis and transcription after a transfer, and make our transfer learning trained models accessible to the public.

Underwater communication systems are increasingly utilized for various purposes, from data transmission to monitoring, but their effectiveness can be significantly hindered by underwater debris. This thesis proposes a novel engineering solution to this problem by developing a robotic cleaning agent capable of operating in complex, unsuitable environments. The agent's navigation and decision-making processes are guided by an SPGP-SARSA policy, while its path is defined using a efficient geometric method known as S4 curve. To enhance efficiency in policy execution and reduce search times in policy evaluation, a innovative data structure called SPGP based on a binary tree is introduced. This structure enables efficient retrieval of actions based on distance thresholds and incorporates a innovative approach based on an SA algorithm for evaluating the effectiveness of the structure. Through simulation experiments, the proposed solution demonstrates its ability to efficiently locate actions, accurately value states and evaluate the performance of the algorithm. These results also illustrate the beneficial impact of the SA algorithm in optimizing the structure and improving the overall performance of the system.

To solve a broad class of relativistic stellar models involving two fluid components with interaction, we found that their solution can be derived from a single-fluid solution by replacing physical quantities with a linear combination and adding a specific term to the conservation laws. We examined multiple cases, discovering that previously reported multi-fluid models can be found within this framework, and it also includes the finding by Bhar and Shukla as a special instance. We then presented two concrete examples with exact solutions, including the extension of a solution by Sahoo and Jhinga, and we discussed the physical and thermodynamic characteristics of these solutions.

Text evaluation tasks, such as spelling correction, often face a barrier when it comes to adapting models to new languages, particularly due to the limited amount of data available in these languages. In this research, we address this challenge by developing a cross-lingual adaptation method for sequence labeling that incorporates an auxiliary task. To accommodate varying language relationships and data amounts, our framework is flexible and can employ shared subnetworks, shared attention mechanisms, or completely isolated structures. We specifically developed three adaptation methods and tested them for English GEC adaptation on a low-resource scale. The results show significant performance gains, with accuracy improvements ranging from 0.5 to 1 point across different settings. Notably, our approach outperforms traditional multi-task transfer learning methods and establishes a new state-of-the-art GEC standard in this specific scenario.

We introduce two novel variants of the classic cut-and-choose cake division algorithm, incorporating a round-robin element and successfully integrate them into an annualized market maker framework. Our first algorithm, combining round-robin and cut-and-choose principles, provides a simplified approach achieving comparable fairness guarantees to the original cut-and-choose algorithm while adhering to the discrete DHR model. Our second algorithm, inspired by the round-robin and cut-and-choose principles, yields a solution meeting the fairness standards of the original cut-and-choose algorithm, while also conforming to the continuous UPE model. Furthermore, both algorithms can be adapted into market maker algorithms, satisfying the desirable properties of anonymity, symmetry, and regularity, as well as unbiasedness and positive earnings regulation. Lastly, in the context of optimal mechanism design with private values, both algorithms emerge as mechanism maximizers.

We have analyzed the optical spectra of the GTC instrument obtained in UGC 8839, a star-forming region in the OMC1 galaxy, using a 1.25-meter effective aperture. The spectra cover a wide range of positions from the galaxy's center to its edges. When compared to other star-forming regions, UGC 8839's HII region population is concentrated at larger distances from the galaxy's center. The galaxy's gas rotation curve and mass distribution were also examined using the SAM and RIGID models. The results show that the mass-to-lightness ratio drops at greater distances, and the galaxy's outer regions have flat rotation curves and high stellar densities.

Using state-of-the-art QCD lattice data, we've reconstructed the behavior of pion masses in response to quark mass changes and found them to be nearly straight lines over a wide range. These findings are supported by both chiral perturbation theory and a simple relativistic hadron resonance gas model. As evidence mounts for a lattice QCD mass variation matching the nucleon to delta resonance ratio of roughly 1.2 to 1.4, our results indicate that pion decay into softer components contributes minimally, explaining why the pion to nucleon ratio remains nearly linear as seen in (anti)deconfining phase transitions. This also suggests the $M_\pi^2\propto\sigma$ Gell-Mann Oakes Renner relation has little impact on hadron behavior near the phase transition temperature.

Researchers used high-resolution spectra from 2018 to study accretion in CT Tau, a classical T Tauri star, by combining the results with previous studies from 2014 and 2020. The study found that accretion rates in CT Tau varied significantly, from $0.15$ to $0.95 M_{\odot} yr^{-1}$, with the atmosphere's ionization not fully understood due to the rapid changes. Additionally, the results showed that while accretion models with single and broad lines were similar in mass, the range of accretion rates in 2014 and 2020 were not well understood. The research called for continued monitoring of the star's accretion rates over time.

In the area of reference-based learning, SIT achieves significant performance improvements, surpassing current methods by more than 20% in challenging tasks, while also enhancing performance in other tasks and overcoming agent identification challenges without pretraining or special training.  The effectiveness of SIT is demonstrated by its ability to exceed current methods in a variety of complex and dynamic multi-agent learning environments, including simulation-based learning with multiple connected agents, reference-based learning with discrete policy spaces, and highly dynamic and complex multi-agent learning environments, all without prior knowledge.

Quantum mechanics raises nonlocal questions through its consistent 'shut-up-and-calculate' approach, yet a deeper understanding emerges when viewing single-particle entanglement as a form of local correlation. This is illustrated via the classic double-slit experiment, in which a single particle becomes entangled with the slits, creating conditions for the experiment to yield informative outcomes. When the slits have disparate scattering properties and the particle's wavelength is sufficiently small, the resulting interference pattern reveals an asymmetry indicative of single-particle steering – the capacity to describe one slit quantumatically based on measurement results from the other slit. To achieve this, we analyze the experiment using both the density matrix and path integral methods, interpreting single-particle correlations as inherently linked to nonclassical behavior.

The integration of Blockchain technology into IoT Vehicles (IoVs) systems has gained significant attention recently, as it promises to enhance both data security and privacy while facilitating reliable interactions between vehicles and infrastructure. Despite the potential advantages offered by Blockchain, several challenges remain in its application within IoVs environments, particularly related to performance limitations, scalability concerns, and compromised efficiency. This paper delves deeper into these difficulties by examining key areas including transaction confirmation delays, gas fees, bandwidth requirements, and storage constraints associated with Blockchain systems. It also explores various proposed solutions that aim to optimize Blockchain-based protocols for improved performance within IoVs settings. Furthermore, this work surveys existing research on the application of Blockchain technology to secure and reliable vehicle communications, as well as to enhance the safety and reliability of autonomous vehicles. A novel classification scheme for Blockchain protocols is also presented, as this work organizes existing solutions based on how they address performance issues, storage management, and the creation of Blockchain networks within IoVs environments. This paper serves as a comprehensive guide to Blockchain-based protocols, offering valuable insights and research directions for both this work and future studies.

The feedback encoding scheme in current wireless systems relies on base stations assessing their individual needs and determining how many bits to request, an inefficient process that doesn't account for the interconnected nature of network elements. In this letter, we introduce an autonomous feedback encoding scheme that leverages deep neural networks to determine the variables a base station transmits. This innovative approach enables bases to independently train and deploy their own models, without the need for coordination. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our method, along with traditional Lloyd clustering, achieves significant improvements, a factor of P network elements, in pilot overhead when deployed.

We have also discovered that these currents retain their robustness in more complex scalar and spinor field cases, containing both bound and tunneling components on the surface of the material structure. These findings have significant implications that may be observable in experiments involving trapped and tunneling field particles.

This study focuses on secure beamforming in an interference-sensitive network, specifically investigating joint optimization of beamforming alignment and power distribution to enhance overall system security. We formulate a min-max problem that aims to minimize the maximum vulnerability across all network users. To address this challenge, we develop an iterative algorithm to achieve near-optimal solutions, and analyze how varying network conditions influence the effectiveness of separate power allocation versus joint optimization approaches. Our results reveal that reorderable user transmission rates are acceptable only under specific constraints related to transmit powers and pathloss, and that joint power allocation is necessary to maintain flexibility when conditions change. To provide clarity on these findings, we compare the network behavior under separate and joint allocation using simulation studies. Our analysis suggests that separate allocation generally yields lower overall security compared to joint allocation, with security implications varying across different users. To support these studies, we incorporate real-world data on wireless communication speeds and distances.

In its broader interpretation, it helps clarify why the WD mass is less than its constituent electrons and nucleons' combined mass, or why a stable bound state's charged particle mass is less than a free particle's mass.  This concept also supports the formulation of the WGC in AdS spaces.  In this paper, we investigate the self-binding energy of a free scalar field in AdS$_{n}$ spaces using the scalar field's charge as a measure.  By deriving an exact expression, we then obtain numerical results for various field masses and AdS$_{n}$ depths.  In ad AdS$_{n}$ spaces, the ratio of a free scalar field's self-binding energy to its charge squared converges to its value in flat space as fields become more massive, or as fields become weakerly coupled in deeply curved AdS$_{n}$ spaces.  By providing this analysis, the work could have implications for understanding the WGC in AdS$_{n}$ spaces.

This research paper proposes a comprehensive framework that integrates the decision-making processes of individual power generators and the management strategies of electrical operators into a unified model. We investigate the occurrence of blow-up in $L^{1+\epsilon}(\Omega)$ for solutions of the Schrödinger equation in a bounded, smooth, convex domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^3$, specifically for the problem:
$$
\begin{cases}
\partial_t u - \Delta u = |u|^p f(p,u) & \text{in } (0,T) \times \Omega, \\
u = 0 & \text{on } (0,T) \times \partial \Omega,
\end{cases}
$$
where $p>5$. It is worth noting that interior blow-up points can be derived from the Pohozaev identity, yet the situation becomes more intricate due to the influence of the domain's boundary. In this context, we establish that the Schrödinger semi-group can map a suitable function space $X$ into the orthogonal complement of the closure of test functions with compact support in $\Omega$, thereby enabling a proof of external blow-up points for the equation. Consequently, we are able to establish the set of external blow-up points is identical to the set of all points on the closure of $\Omega$.

This research extends the principle of symmetric multi-fold vector bundles to the symplectical domain by introducing a symmetric $n$-fold vector bundle framework. In this paper, we establish a connection between two mathematical frameworks: the Kirillov measure and geometric measure on certain algebraic structures. We show that for a specific type of group, the relationship between these two measures can be expressed as an equality involving an integral equation with a unknown function. This equation contains additional terms represented by unknown functions, whose number varies depending on the algebraic structure in question.

This research involves applying a phase retrieval algorithm to real x-ray scattering data, specifically energy scattering curves from an 8-beam x-ray interferometer. A new method is proposed for calculating phase errors from these curves, which is more efficient than traditional approaches. The algorithm is also improved for handling noisy data, and its effectiveness is demonstrated through the reconstruction of an x-ray energy spectrum from a scattering curve. Additionally, it is shown how this technique can be used to enhance the measurement of beam flux density, and as such, an in-depth discussion on this application is provided.

The study aims to develop a directed percolation model that effectively represents the complex interactions in fractured porous media with blocked cracks. To achieve this, a new function, Dirac-$\eta$, is introduced and its properties investigated in relation to blockage dynamics. The research demonstrates that the Dirac-$\eta$ function can provide a valuable tool for modeling spatial-temporal variations in permeability. Furthermore, findings from experiments with different injection rates can be expressed as an injection-rate directed percolation model. Notably, the approach reveals that injecting data at multiple points can be equivalent to injecting a single composite channel. However, this equivalence does not always hold when examining the structure of fluid flow within the medium.

Rule-based systems for making decisions under uncertainty have been used successfully in various applications, but they require hand-tuned rules and simple hypothesis selection methods that may limit their performance. In contrast, learning a rule-based model from data allows for a more compact and human-interpretable representation that incorporates prior knowledge. To address the problem of selecting the best hypothesis from a set of candidates, we introduce a differential utility function (DUF) framework that enables a more precise evaluation by assigning functions to compare differences in outcomes rather than absolute values. We develop an algorithm called UDTI (Utility Decision Tree Induction) that learns DUFs interactively through a series of questions with a human operator. UDTI focuses on identifying regions where specific behaviors are expected, rather than absolute outcomes, and we incorporate this principle into our algorithm. We evaluate UDTI on synthetic and real-world datasets, showing a performance improvement of up to 10% in test accuracy compared to standard decision tree methods, while requiring significantly fewer questions to reach high accuracy.

Understanding the connections between the parts of a complex idea is a crucial aspect of human communication, yet this is significantly hampered by a lack of structured data representing the relationships between different sentence segments. We are proposing a comprehensive and multi-dimensional resource to address this challenge, starting with a vast set of potential links between sentences and continuing with possible sentence-to-segment connections. At the sentence-level, we have created a large dataset called DiscSense, consisting of 1.2 million pairs of related sentences embedded in short text passages, which are manually verified by humans. Understanding the potential discursive and causal relationships within a given paragraph is made easier with this dataset, and we have also established a benchmark for tasks involving discourse marker classification and classification of these relationships. To facilitate a deeper analysis, we have also established a possible distinction between discursive and causal relationships, as well as possible alternatives to a purely semantic understanding of the connections at play.

This paper examines the geodesic strong convexity and smoothness properties of objective functions evaluated on a factorized matrix space within the context of low-rank matrix optimization problems. Utilizing these characterizations, we analyze and compare the convergence rates of gradient descent methods on the primary variable versus updates on the matrix factors, demonstrating that in certain settings, the algorithm on the primary variable achieves a convergence rate equivalent to gradient descent on the primary variable itself. Furthermore, we provide concrete examples that illustrate the application of our main results.

Postulating that for any bipartite graph with a maximum edge degree of $\Delta$, the strong edge-coloring requires at least $\sqrt[3]{2}\Delta^2$ distinct colors holds true. Initially verified in 1990 by Erdős et al. that it would hold for any graph requiring $c(G)$ distinct colors in a specific scenario, it was later refuted by Bartoniček and Sgerd in 2017 for a specific type of bipartite graph with a maximum edge degree 3, which has 9 vertices in its higher degree partition. A strong edge-coloring for this particular case, this bipartite graph can be accomplished with 10 distinct colors, was demonstrated. Moreover, it was established that for such graphs, coloring them strongly with at most $f(\Delta)$ distinct colors is possible.

This study employs co-evolutionary genetic algorithms to conduct experiments on a Rock Paper Scissors game, allowing agents to develop optimal strategies through the development and assessment of action-frequency vectors. The results reveal that when action selection follows the uniform random distribution, a unique strategy emerges as the only Nash Equilibrium. Conversely, for non-zero payoffs in Rock Paper Scissors, learning leads to action-frequency vectors exceeding the expected Hamming distance from any Nash Equilibrium uniform random distribution. For a payoff value of 1 in Rock Paper Scissors, this expected hamming distance is larger in the social learning case than in the individual learning case, which can be ascribed to individual learning adhering to the pure strategy Nash Equilibria whereas the unique Nash Equilibrium uniform random distribution is the only one reached by the social learning. The findings of this study are limited by the reliance on simple games and should be expanded upon through the investigation of more complex games coupled with sophisticated learning mechanisms.

Consider a weighted oriented graph $\mathcal{O}(G)$ built upon a weighted undirected graph $G$, within a polynomial ring with two variables. We demonstrate that under specific conditions, where the set of weights associated with the directed edges forms an interval, the ordinary symbolic power equals the symbolic power for a given natural number j of the ideal associated with this structure. This equality holds when comparing the j-th ordinary symbolic power to the j-th symbolic power in the context of a given weight distribution. This equality is examined and characterized with respect to the given structure. Furthermore, we investigate and compare the ordinary symbolic powers and the symbolic powers of this structure.

Various techniques such as dropout and weight corruption have been proposed to improve the resilience and performance of neural networks in their training phase. In contrast, silencing data corruptions, which secretly modify network inputs during training without the trainee's knowledge, have been shown to effectively train on convincing deception and result in disastrous failures when deployed. In this paper, we introduce a novel method to prevent silent data corruptions, called Non-Uniform Range Restriction (NARR). Our method forces detection of silent data corruptions and neutralizes their impact, even in extreme cases. To accomplish this, we identify the characteristics of silencing data corruptions and then implement a detection mechanism using minimal resources. Our proposal is evaluated on both image and text data sets and proves to be successful in our experiments.

We have established that the generalization of the Jordanian twist for the $r$-matrix can be derived from the basic Jordanian twist through an $r$-coecient automorphism, maintaining its property under multiple derivations. As a direct application, the Jordanian twist associated with the $r$-matrix in multiple parameters can be expressed using the basic Jordanian twist and two differential operators.

The challenge of tagging names in low-resource languages has been exacerbated by the limited availability of annotated data for these languages. To address this limitation, this paper proposes a method that leverages pre-trained multilingual language models and semi-supervised learning techniques. By employing a self-adaptive masking strategy and a series of loss functions, the proposed approach enhances the tagging of names in languages with limited resources. Experimental results on multiple languages demonstrate the superiority of the proposed method over state-of-the-art baselines, particularly in languages with scarce data.

This research examines various pair combinations of light flavor hadron pairs, specifically kaon/triagon, proton/antiproton, and net proton to antiproton ratios, observed across different collisions including central Au+Au, Cu+Cu, and Pb+Pb events at the energy level of 7.2 TeV. Notable patterns in these ratios in relation to system size have been theoretically explained through the interplay of transport processes and hadton formation.

The recent 2019 Nepal Earthquake triggered significant infrastructure damage and power outages in multiple Indian states, sparking a strong political reaction from the Nepalese Prime Minister and contributing to the dissolution of the Nepalese Parliament. This series of interconnected events – from the earthquake to the Indian riots and ultimately the political changes in Nepal – highlights the potential influence of a city's infrastructure network on the spread of civil unrest. In this study, we develop a model that incorporates infrastructure connections between cities to simulate the spread of unrest influenced by social media, and we use the 'betweenness centrality' measure to identify key infrastructure nodes that, if targeted, could help contain the effects of riots in neighboring regions.

This work proposes a new optimal control framework for deep learning-based Vision-Inertial Optimization (VIO) models. The developed framework utilizes an elementary data representation method, allowing gradient-descent-based training for comprehensive and non-linear constraints, including camera dynamics, sensor measurements, and IoT device data. Formulating the optimizer as an ultimate learning (UL) problem, we determine the ideal controller weights by jointly optimizing controller weights and controller architecture in a manner that minimizes trajectory deviation from the actual system data under future conditions. Future research will explore extensive domains such as multi-agent optimal control with deep VIO replaceable by our model for uniform data processing and element representation, as well as potential extensions to our framework for controller architecture determination and deep learning-based model applications in constrained multi-agent optimal control problems.

We investigate higher-order Weyl semimetals in three dimensions, exploring their rich topological features and higher-order Willett monopoles at the boundary. We illustrate various topological invariants including a 2D index, a 1D index, and a 3D index that characterize this complex ground state. We examine theoretical models, analyzing a Hamiltonian with parabolic dispersion and more complex cases, including both single and multiple Weyl monopoles. We further investigate the stability of higher-order Weyl semimetric phases under intrinsic index protection against scattering. We describe scattering behavior of electrons in these system, which is influenced by index, leading to a characteristic combination of higher-order helicity and valley hall effects. We illustrate these effects using a four-band four-layer model, providing its tight-binding Hamiltonian and calculating the topological index using numerical simulations.

This research paper presents a novel numerical method for Data Completion problems, combining an optimization approach with an appropriate numerical discretization technique. We focus on edge finite elements, which offer significant advantages in handling such issues. Our study demonstrates that using a first-order edge elements framework provides several benefits, including enhanced accuracy in gradients near missing data areas, precise recovery of data in these regions, and insensitivity to the scale of data absence. Our findings are supported by supportive numerical results from multiple experiments.

Knowledge models are frequently disrupted by inaccurate or conflicting factual updates, necessitating a seamless integration method that can incorporate such information. In this work, a new saliency-aware distillation approach is proposed to facilitate efficient integration, focusing on a way to amalgamate knowledge from various teachers into a more comprehensive student model. By prioritizing knowledge from the most informative teacher models during the training process, a mechanism is devised that can灵活ly adapt to various teacher models with differing levels of reliability and expertise. To facilitate this, a saliency-based approach is employed to instruct a student model to learn from the more informative aspects of teacher models. To evaluate its effectiveness, several amalgamation tasks were conducted on diverse datasets, and the results show a significant performance boost of nearly 2.5 PPTs when compared to a base distillation method. Additionally, our approach demonstrates a significant improvement in robustness and generalizability. Furthermore, an analysis of our approach reveals that an increased salience of loss corresponds to a more diverse repertoire of assembled models.

Using the elliptic curve $E: <1,-1,0,0,0>$ defined over $\mathbb{Q}$ with current rational rank 0 as a starting point, we investigate the extensive collection of $S_4$ quartic extensions $K \subset \mathbb{Q}[x]/S_4$ where $K$ allows $E$ to acquire higher rank in the Mordell-Weil group $Ellp(K)/S_4$ without increasing the original rank of $E$ in $Ellp(\mathbb{Q})$. It is notably established that within the set of $S_4$ quartic fields, there are infinitely many instances where $E$ can increase its rank from 0 to 1 without altering its 2-torsion structure, thus providing a concrete example of an elliptic curve that becomes rank 1 in certain quartic fields.

Quantum quenches in $1+1$-dimensional, continuous-time, discrete-spin, interacting systems initially prepared in thermal equilibrium can result in out-of-equilibrium states whose properties can be characterized by temperature and entropy production. By using Monte Carlo methods to track the evolution of these properties, we can determine the transition point for when the quadrupole moment of a probe particle's distribution indicates a sharp, non-analytic change associated with a continuous phase transition. This analysis reveals that the quench parameters at which this transition occurs can be precisely determined, revealing the underlying mechanism of the phase transition.

We present an alternative perspective on the time after which an environment can validly be treated as a separate entity from a newly prepared quantum system's degrees of freedom. By applying a time-twirling operation to the joint system-environment state, our approach yields a unified connection between the point at which the system can be effectively decoupled from the environment and the time when a specific non-equilibrium phenomenon, known as time, arises. Our findings indicate that decoupling and the emergence of this "decoupling time" can equivalently be described through the same mathematical framework, providing a pathway to estimate when it may be acceptable to disregard the environment's influence on the system's subsequent non-unitary evolution, including intriguing scenarios such as non-linear quantum dynamics.

A regular simplex is characterized by its vertices being equidistant from one another. This research explores how simplexes used in interpolation can contribute to data science, specifically by examining nondegenerate regular simplexes within a unit cube. The condition for the existence of these simplexes is found to be satisfied when the number of interpolation nodes is greater than half their square minus half their root, yet less than half their square minus half their root. Furthermore, ways to construct a nondegenerate regular simplex are shown for any suitable number of interpolation nodes, beginning with an example where a three-dimensional regular simplex can be formed using two nodes. The paper also provides an algorithm to generate any nondegenerate regular simplex, and discusses how these simplexes can be utilized in weighted barycentric coordinate interpolation.

Etched silicon (ES) has been examined with respect to its etching process, 
and in comparison with buffer oxide etched silicon (BOES).  The etching of 
silicon was carried out in two different ways: etched in buffer (EB) and 
dry etched silicon (DEBS).  In both cases, the silicon was completely 
depleted of carriers.  In contrast, silicon that was dry etched in the 
absence of a self-limiting oxide layer exhibited a high level of 
carrier concentration (>10^12 cm^-3).  SiES samples were prepared by 
removing the surface layer through etching.  These samples showed 
approximately 10^11 cm^-3 of n-type carriers, predominantly located 
within a depth range of 5 nm.  These results are significant for 
ultra-large-scale integration applications, especially in relation to 
dual die-with-interconnect technology.  Such applications require a high 
degree of carrier concentration along the cut surface.

Interior-exterior cycling within planetary systems is a crucial driver with deep implications for the trajectory of a planet's atmospheric evolution over time. To fully comprehend the evolution of exoplanetary atmospheres, it is essential to account for the interactions between a planet's interior and exterior. This study conducts a detailed analysis of Venus's atmospheric evolution by integrating the planet's interior and exterior dynamics within the same model. We employed a multi-dimensional general circulation model to simulate the Venusian atmosphere while simultaneously modeling the planet's magnetic field, geothermal energy, and surface $CO_2$ and water vapor content to explore the long-term evolution of the atmosphere. The results reveal that despite our inclusion of energy and angular momentum recycling between the atmosphere and interior, the model fails to prevent the atmosphere from becoming overly heated and thickened by nearly 100 times, a common outcome in previous one-dimensional studies. Additionally, we investigate the potential for the broken magnetic shield to contribute to the enhanced atmospheric escape, a process that also fails to stop the atmosphere from escaping to its present state. To better understand how the atmosphere reached its current condition and to develop escape mechanisms capable of balancing the flux and avoiding runaway greenhouse conditions, further research is necessary.

The multivariate Hawkes process, a non-linear point process model that captures complex interaction phenomena, has found applications in various fields such as geophysics, finance, and the study of online content like news and social media. However, modeling these contents often involves large data sets, necessitating efficient modeling tools. While the standard Hawkes process is based on the Poisson distribution and lacks the capacity to model intricate contents, this paper presents a generalized model using the nonlinear Hawkes process. The paper outlines various estimation methods, simulated examples, and real-world applications, including modeling comment threads and presenting estimated kernel functions that represent the interactions between different user contents.

A new technique for linear circular polarization transformation is proposed, utilizing a plasma medium as a waveplate. The required thickness of the plasma is significantly thinner than that of traditional Fermi-waveplates, making it suitable for high-energy applications. The conditions for effective operation are analyzed, with a focus on the relationship between necessary thickness, electron density, and magnetic field strength. Examples of efficient high-density plasma channel configurations are provided, including those created using neutral gas discharge and laser-produced channels in high-density solid state targets. The discussion includes an examination of plasma channel dynamics and strategies to minimize electron density channel profiles while maintaining zero-cryogenic rotation.

This paper investigates the error correction capabilities of rank metric codes, which have various applications and are characterized by the dimension of the subspace perpendicular to a given vector. We find that such codes exhibit an asymmetric error correction capability, which is further influenced by a code's rank metric distance. Specifically, we prove that codes with a ratio of their minimum rank metric distance to their vector space's dimension greater than 1/2 can correct a larger subset of errors that is determined by the codes' distance, in contrast to codes with a ratio less than 1/2 that exhibit asymmetric error correction capabilities without a connection to the codes' distance. We also provide a new construction of these codes with a ratio greater than 1/2 using matrix transformation.

Neutron stars and black holes are primarily created through core-collapse supernovAs and SN-like events.  In order to better understand the complexities of nucleosynthesis in these occurrences, extensive observations of SN~2020jfo's spectral lines were conducted using the 9.1-meter Subaru Telescope.  By analyzing the broad absorption features in its spectrum, key ratios of Ni/Fe, N/Si, and O/Si were determined to be 1.94, 2.55, and 1.41 respectively.  These values provide a ni/Fe production ratio of 1.41, a lower value than the SN1987A ratio of 5.45 and closer to the overall CCSN estimated range of 1-10.  Furthermore, the Ni/Fe and N/Si values are also less than the values of 4.0 and 4.2 respectively, found in the interstellar medium.  This implies that additional processes are required to explain the levels of Ni and N present in the universe.  In summary, SN~2020jfo's spectrum offers a detailed and unique viewpoint on the features of massive star collapses.  Therefore, it remains an invaluable resource for the study of nucleosynthesis and the formation of compact objects.

We analyzed the cross-shaped image produced by a particular segment of a lobster-eye optics system located at the focal area of a specific telescope. By observing the image's rotation across different exposures, we were able to determine the angular position of each individual mirror within the cross-shaped pattern with an accuracy of approximately 10 degrees. The relationship between the azimuthal rotation angle and the angular position of the mirror follows a simple and direct proportionality, which allows us to easily interpret the results. This finding enables us to identify the exact location of each mirror, offering a useful method for monitoring any shifts in the subarray's position.

Our method involves defining the operator $p\mapsto P(\vp)$ and nonlinear term $f$ through level set methods, also known as max-pooling. Our method offers a way to solve the nonlinear equation implicitly, by determining the solution map $p\mapsto \vp$ and the domain $\Omega$ from boundary conditions, without inverting the equation explicitly. We also discuss applications to dynamic programming principles and optimal stopping problems.

Unlike conventional variables that attribute mass and angular momentum as properties of mass units, our approach defines the location of fluid elements based on their mass and specific angular momentum. Through a mathematical transformation and a linearized approximation of the complex forces at play, we derive a unique set of trigonometric equations that describe the star's differential rotation. By applying the boundary conditions of the specific angular momentum, we determine the precise value of the integration constant and a different differential equation. This equation is similar to a previously studied equation in general stellar theory, and unlike its predecessor, it can be solved to find the star's angular velocity.

In recent years, neutron stars have become a focal point of research due to
the significant coalescence events they produce, which yield substantial
gravitational and electromagnetic radiation for analysis. By combining these
two types of data, scientists can gain the most comprehensive understanding
possible of these events. To illustrate this potential, we focus on a specific
event, GW190521, where observations indicated that the gravitational and
electromagnetic signals were seen during a brief, bright phase of its evolution,
which could have been caused by the formation of a massive, rapidly spinning
neutron star or even a black hole, before collapsing. We show that various
electromagnetic events, including those resulting from interactions with
relativistic jets, the surrounding disk, or through shock waves, could have
led to the events seen by us as a short-pulsar, with each event leaving
characteristic patterns that can help guide future research. Furthermore, we
demonstrate that by analyzing the events seen by us with data from various
observatories, it is theoretically possible to gain a detailed understanding
of the events events, the events' environment, and the events' precursor
stages. However, in order to achieve this, we need to overcome significant
barriers in order to detect the events' signals in the gamma-ray, X-ray, and
radio frequency ranges.

The pandemic and related containment measures significantly altered how diverse urban environments bring people together and impacted a community's ability to recover. While previous studies have examined these changes, they often suffered from limited scope, duration, and varied contexts. This paper offers an overview of the effects of the pandemic on urban diversity and community resilience by highlighting both commonalities and differences in experiences across multiple cities, as well as the opportunities and challenges for urban planning and resilience efforts. Ultimately, this discussion aims to stimulate a more thorough debate on necessary actions for advancing diverse and resilient cities.

The inner regions of the solar system were shaped by a crowded and unstable disk that also influenced the dynamics of the young Sun. Near high-mass stellar objects, very small planets could form within their warm and dusty environments. However, these planets would be displaced as they migrated through the system. In order to test our understanding of these planet interactions, high-precision observations of stellar positions are being used to detect small, migrating objects around young high-mass stars. We developed a computational model to simulate the movements of multiple planets that are trapped in a disc around a high-mass star, using direct gravitational interactions between the planets and simulating smaller particles as dust or larger objects without detailed physical properties. Our simulations showed that small, migrating planets could exist in stable configurations for extended periods, although their movements were highly irregular and unpredictable due to random interactions with migrating bodies. We found that the inner disk could exhibit complex dynamics with periods of relative stability and periods of disorder that displaced objects outward. Our findings also revealed that migrating objects could enter a relative quiescence near the star, allowing for the detection of them through precise observations of the star's movement, before experiencing sudden increases in their orbital radii. We believe that interpreting these observations can provide us with a deeper understanding of the formations of planetary systems around high-mass stars.

A numerical method based on high-order spectral transformation is developed to calculate horizontal and vertical water surface properties from given wave envelope and phase information. This approach contrasts traditional techniques that determine total energy from surface properties, flipping the calculation process. The proposed model's accuracy was tested through various case studies and a known depth-dependent energy distribution formula, demonstrating its efficacy in resolving the surface elevation reconstruction problem. Especially beneficial for deep water scenarios where measuring internal properties is challenging, this method offers a convenient computational alternative to physical measurements.

A significant issue in automated systems is real-time obstacle detection and avoidance. A novel layered control system is proposed to address this issue on a mobile platform, which is equipped with a rotating sonar sensor and aims to safely navigate around static and moving obstacles in an unstructured setting. The platform's sonar device rapidly identifies and classifies the spacing between nearby, static and moving obstacles in real-time, enabling the control system to prioritize avoiding collisions with them. A external shell-based safety layer, which relies on open-loop dynamics models and feed-back sonar readings, ensures that the platform maintains a sufficient distance from all detected obstacles. A navigation layer, which uses a sonar-based view of the environment, directs the platform to maneuver through available gaps and seize any clear paths as they become accessible. The proposed system was successfully tested in various lab and home-like environments, as well as with another autonomous platform, and a recorded data set from a home-like environment is also released for research purposes.

This study presents a model for identifying sensitive and deceptive online content, particularly within the context of emergencies, where time-sensitive and private information play crucial roles. We constructed an urgent, authentic, and deceptive news detection system called UAD, utilizing a multi-task learning approach that prioritizes critical information and incorporates contextual elements to represent the most informative words and contextual patterns to enhance model performance. Our results show that the proposed UAD model significantly surpasses current state-of-the-art methods in detecting sensitive content, particularly when combined with an attention-based mechanism for learning and contextual information when performance gains are most pronounced.

This paper addresses the $l_1$-PCA optimization problem with two variable blocks following a rotationally invariant transformation. We present an algorithm based on coordinate descent using alternating minimization. By simplifying one variable block at a time, we develop an iterative algorithm. We prove the reformulated problem allows for an equivalent solution to the original. Specifically, we discuss two approaches: solving the problem with two continuous variable blocks using ADMM, and applying coordinate descent when there are discrete and continuous variable blocks. We analyze convergence and provide proof for our proposed algorithm. Numerical results demonstrate the efficiency of our method and provide visualizations of clustered principal components from real-world data.

This paper introduces a novel approach to semantic labeling annotation, incorporating a paraphrase detection task to verify the accuracy of annotated labels. This method incorporates a single additional step where an expert validates the human-generated label by ensuring its consistency with the gold standard. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, we collected a dataset called Visual Phrase-Base Consistency (VP-Base), consisting of 5000 manually verified examples from the Visual Phrase-Test set. Our HiTMap representation combines hierarchical local-to-global coordinates for effective robot navigation. It enables straightforward position translation between local and global realms while enabling query and update operations within the global metric map without intricate reorganization. We've developed a method to integrate sensory inputs using only local components, yet we show that under specific conditions, learned policies can generalize to the entire environment without retraining. Using a simulated scenario, it is demonstrated that with the HiTMap representation, the navigation task can be effectively solved. It is further shown that both representation and map contents can be learned using only negative feedback from the environment. When tested on a real robot, our approach shows that it can solve previously unknown tasks and requires significantly simpler sensory inputs, solely in the form of actions and states.

To improve sensitivity by several orders of magnitude, techniques were demonstrated to reduce this noise ratio to 6 and 0. 6, in optical loop feedback and radio-frequency atom detection methods, respectively, at modulation frequencies of one Hertz and ten Hertz.

The number of components in mixture models is typically fixed, which does not suit many applications. While Bayesian methods allow flexibility by placing DP prior on densities, the issue of identifying interpretable admixture weights remains unresolved when the component count is predetermined. This paper demonstrates that DP methods can also be used for estimations and shows that posterior samples of covariates can recover a matrix of bases that contains DP bases as a subset, when using a specific transformation to represent admixture weights. Furthermore, this property does not hold when using the most common simplex transformations, which implies the need for alternative approaches. A new transformation called the Neyman-Scott (NS) prior density is presented in this process, demonstrating that it retains the property of recovering DP bases as a subset while also being capable of inferring the number of components with a meaningful precision.

The exploration of simulation options for complex systems is a critical step in defining their control algorithms, especially for autonomous vehicles. Due to device programming on GPUs being extensively utilized for simulation, efficient GPU memory allocation becomes crucial. However, GPU memory managers for allocation algorithms like reference counting and generational garbage collection often experience performance drops from global memory barriers and memory reallocation. Existing solutions like `cudaMalloc` and custom allocators in popular simulation frameworks often incur high memory allocation and barrier overheads, resulting in data loss or unnecessary simulations. We developed DynaSOAr, a GPU memory manager that employs an dynamic segmentation strategy to reduce memory barriers and enhance reallocation efficiency, allowing for simultaneous garbage collection and GCS without additional memory barriers, thus improving performance and allowing for safer pointer updates. Our tests demonstrate that DynaSOAr can cut 50 to as much as $6.0 \times 10^2$ percent of memory barriers and 3.3 to as much as $10.0 \times 10^0$ percent of CPU time on memory allocation, across four different GPU sizes while working with popular simulation libraries like Gazebo and Webots.

We investigated the interaction between a d-wave superconductor and magnetic adatoms or dimers with varying spin-orbit coupling strengths. By analyzing local density of states near the Fermi level, we found that the superconducting gap is present near the impurity but is reduced in the vicinity of the (2,0) site due to the anisotropy of the d-wave order parameter. We also observed that the positions of peaks associated with YSR states remain unaffected by the spin-orbit coupling near the (1,0) site. However, increasing the strength of spin-orbit coupling causes the peaks near the (2,0) site to shift and eventually causes the middle peak to disappear. At a critical threshold, the spin-orbit coupling becomes strong enough to change the superconducting ground state from nodal to nodeless and causes a phase transition in the system.

The substitution of Ti with C and N in the TiO2 (110) surface has been examined, along with the properties of C and N in interstitial positions. The presence of a magnetic moment arises from spin polarization at the (110) surface when a specific type of interstitial C exists, with its strength being 2 times greater than in a (001) surface.

Top quark decays into other types of quarks through a flavor changing neutral current are strictly prohibited by the Standard Model due to its conservation laws, making such decays crucial for detecting new, exotic physics beyond the Standard Model at high-energy particle colliders like the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) and the Future Circular Collider (FCC). This paper explores two processes involving top quarks producing other quarks through flavor changing neutral currents that involve significant hadronic radiation, specifically focusing on final states with significant hadronic radiation paired with a photon or a W boson and then proposes strategies for searching for these processes in top quark pair production at the LHC with the ATLAS experiment at center-of-mass energies of 13 and 100 TeV. Analyses demonstrate that in low new physics coupling regimes, the most precise measurements of such decay branching ratios can be achieved in top quark pair production processes with a 100 TeV collider offering 30 ab$^{-1}$ of data, where branching ratio limits for the $t \to \mathrm{charm} + \text{nothing}$ decay could reach the 10$^{-8}$ range and for the $t \to \mathrm{bottom} + \text{nothing}$ decay, the 10$^{-9}$ range.

We examine decoherence in a quantum phase estimation system, specifically the Aharanov-Lebowitz-Aberbach (ALA) protocol, as it operates within a $1$-dimensional solid-state quantum phase space. Our research focuses on noise effects derived from the Born and Markovian master equation, particularly examining the impact of spectral density on noise characteristics for both discrete frequency levels (qubits) and continuous frequency levels (qutrits). Our analyses utilize three distinct methods: analytical solutions, numerical integration, and numerical differentiation. Our findings demonstrate that qutrits exhibit greater resilience to noise than qubits in the specific context of the ALA protocol within a $1$-dimensional solid-state quantum system, under the examined conditions. Our results are presented in the form of qudit noise tolerance maps, providing a comprehensive overview of parameters that enable effective qutrid phase estimation with reduced noise impact. Our study also explores the effects of different master equation formulations, including non-Markovian and Markovian variations, on the alcohol tolerance in qudit systems.

Recent measurements indicate that the polarization of positrons collected from a $2.5$-GeV electron beam through the $e^+e^-$ pair production process can reach approximately $10$ percent. We demonstrate that direct generation of positrons via the $Bost{\rm edd}$ effect in a high-field ($\sim 10$ kGauss) spiral undulator can yield a polarization degree exceeding 30% for positrons with an energy range of 0.5 to 2 times the peak undulator field strength squared multiplied by $10^{-6}$ (in units of electron rest mass energy). These positrons could then be collected and utilized to enhance the overall polarization of positrons and electrons found in existing and upcoming particle accelerators.

In this research, a novel on-chip temperature monitoring system is presented, featuring a 12-degree Celsius full resolution and a 3.5 Kelvin average error rate per device. The proposed solution, despite its simplified design lacking active feedback, matches the precision of much more accurate reference systems. Achieved by utilizing a highly sensitive MOSFET, this solution offers an improved balance of exactness and speed, resulting in a monitoring rate of 50 cycles per second. The solution also has a low power consumption of 1.2 milliwatts, was developed using a 0.18-micron process technology, and was physically 0.23 square millimeters in size.

Given a topological stack and an $n$-fold topological groupoid composition law, we have developed a method to define topological groupoid extensions as a generalization of bundle constructions. Specifically, for a morphism from a topological stack $\mathcal{X}$ to the quotient of $\mathcal{Y}$ by a groupoid $G$, we can construct canonical bundle-like structures; this process can be viewed as part of a sectioning functor that operates in reverse on categories of higher topological structures. Furthermore, we have demonstrated that this sectioning functor has properties akin to a right adjoint, thus motivating the study of its potential left adjoint, which could be interpreted as a topological version of a monad pseudo-transformations.

We investigated the mass development of molecular cores in space, specifically those with a predicted probability of forming a massive star, and observed their mass growth over time using the ALMA telescope. In contrast, in previous studies, core growth was typically represented by their current state instead of their dynamic evolution. Our analysis utilized the H_2 1-0 line and the CO line, line ratio maps to analyze the molecular core's environment, finding that most cores (six out of nine) continued to accrete mass from their surrounding environment, with a growth rate of at least 0.15 masses per year. In particular, core L1159-E exhibited a high growth rate of at least 1.2 masses per year in a bright, dense disk, likely contributing to the formation of a massive star in the future. In addition, our research demonstrates that transient line ratio maps are an effective method for analyzing the mass growth of molecular cores and predicting which cores have a high probability of forming a massive star, and will be especially valuable as more extensive surveys using next generation facilities like ALMA Phase 2 and NOEMA become available.

We examine whether the operation of integrating or differentiating a positive definite zonal function in direction any given direction preserves its positive definiteness. It turns out this holds for all radial positive definite functions in at least two dimensions, however, when examining these operations against specific measures or when considering specific angles, the result is not always a positive definite function. This examination reveals insights into the impact of integration and differentiation on the properties of zonal functions, with implications for understanding the behavior of positive definite functions under various transformations.

A key parameter that is used to characterize the ability of liquid foams to either settle like a solid block or drain to form thin films is the roughness factor R, which is defined as the ratio of the domain width to its height in a square domain. A significant challenge is creating the roughness factor in simulations, particularly for large values of R, which require scaling effects to be replicated accurately. This paper presents a significant achievement of reaching values of R up to 720, and also explains a new approach to scaling simulations to larger values of R. It is found that two key parameters, which are the capillary number and the Reynolds number, must be kept constant, and the domain's spatial resolution must be adjusted to the size of the bubbles to match the physical behavior of the foams. It is also observed that both free-draining foams, which are characterized by negligible surface tension and gravity, as well as settled foams, which are caused by thickening near the bottom of the domain, can be used as indicators to validate and check the accuracy of the simulations.

Simply CNN ensemble techniques have already seen a substantial performance boost in small-image classification tasks, yet their application has been limited in deep CNN ensemble scenarios due to the high computational cost involved. A significant challenge with single-model CNN ensembles lies in their limited flexibility, as it's extremely difficult to modify an existing classifier without completely rebuilding it. On the other hand, dropout-based CNNs offer the advantage of implicitly creating an ensemble of single models without the need for training or evaluating multiple separate models. In this research, we investigate the potential benefits of deep CNN ensembles, as well as their single-model equivalents, across a wide range of tasks using the same CNN architecture. These tasks include the original indications for CNN ensemble usage, such as small-image classification, as well as more complex applications like semantic segmentation and beyond. To effectively handle these complicated applications in an efficient and versatile manner, we propose a single-model CNN ensemble approach that allows for efficient evaluation of the entire ensemble without requiring the ensembles to be trained on their own. We demonstrate the efficacy of this novel approach on ImageNet with applications extending to human annotation, showing that our flexible single-model CNN ensemble can outperform various benchmark systems.

A lower speed range leads to high-texture states due to membrane tension, whereas a upper speed range causes smooth states to become persistent against rippling. Intermediate speeds allow for easy transitions between these extremes. This model predicts testable relationships between these speed ranges and specific tension-induced speeds.

Our paper proposes a novel look-ahead attention mechanism for neural machine translation, enhancing the basic model by allowing the translation process to anticipate future target tokens. We developed a practical implementation of this technique, called NASA, integrating it into an attention-based translator with no significant computational cost. Our model's look-ahead attention is easily understandable and controllable, facilitating improved training, evaluation, and potential applications such as accelerating translation with no compromise in quality. Our research shows that NASA achieves better performance across multiple language pairs compared to existing controlled generation methods, and also succeeds in recaptifying high-frequency n-grams, benefiting for example from the improved ability to handle low-resource scenarios and phrases that follow common patterns.

The rapid advancement of grid computing technology necessitates a sustainable method of explanation and guidance, which can be achieved through a focus on diverse societal groups' priorities and contexts. The concept of 'translation' in this setting involves creating a shared understanding of objectives among developers, the technology itself, various users, and broader societal contexts. This paper outlines the benefits of applying a translational methodology to the grid computing domain, which is supported by empirical evidence from the development of a public policy management interface within the European Grid Infrastructure. The advantages of this approach are demonstrated through the translation process in action, which is beneficial for creating user-friendly interfaces that bridge technical functionality with real-world implications, as well as for involving users in the grid computing development process through contextualized participation. Ultimately, a translational perspective proves valuable for users, developers, and the grid computing community as a whole.

MFSSA is an advanced version of SSA that uses factor analysis to its advantage. 
Like SSA, MFSSA is a method that is non-parametric and doesn't rely on any model assumptions, 
it does decompose a complex input into its constituent parts that are multiplicative combinations 
of simple linear patterns and non-patternized diagonal components. In this research, we used 
Morlet's transform to replace SSA's T-and-B components in order to create a new method called 
Complex Factor Spectrum Analysis (CFSA). In the training process, we employed backpropagation 
to its variant of T-and-B components which were set as initial networks, in order to match 
the training input. In the testing process, we used these network components to reconstruct 
the input data. MFSSA and CFSA can be utilized in a wide range of applications, including 
analyzing temperature curves and creating smooth time series models, as well as for unsupervised 
noise modeling and image denoising using remote sensing technology.

Let b be a positive value and let X1, X2,... be independent and identically distributed random variables with a common distribution F that is zero-mean. Let Sn represent the sum of these random variables from 1 to n. The asymptotic behavior of the random walk Sn as n approaches infinity, depending on the value of b, is analyzed with respect to a non-decreasing function w in the context of weak convergence modulo lb for b = 1, 2,..., infinity. The main findings are expressed as follows: The random walk scaled by b to the power of 1/2 and divided by the function w, denoted as (Wsn b to the power of 1/2)/w, has a set of asymptotic limits that is equivalent to the set of functions W in the space of continuous functions over the real line, when the distribution of the random variables has a finite variance; However, when the random variables have an infinite variance, the set of asymptotic limits changes, and this is characterized by the function w. The function must satisfy certain conditions specific to each value of b to characterize its asymptotic growth, and these conditions are analyzed in the context of the random walk's distribution.

Understanding the relationship between key indicators, such as electron temperature and density, and a crucial factor, like plate polarity, is essential for improving a specific type of plasma source. This research holds significance for developers of plasma technology by providing a foundation for creating more effective processing chambers with consistent results, rather than relying on trial and error. Also, it is possible to accurately predict the distribution of plasma parameters across various plate positions, which is critical for ensuring consistent results and avoiding potential issues, such as etch profile collapse during a process known as silicon etching. On the onus side, a machine learning model was used to estimate electron temperature and density without the need for a rigorous physical model, which is often difficult to create. This research is unique in that it incorporates the effect of plate polarity into the model, which has not been done before. Furthermore, a high level of accuracy was achieved in estimating both temperature and density, with an average error of 10%. This research is unique in that it paves the way for several applications, such as replacing existing physical models, which can be time-consuming and inaccurate, with more precise simulations, or even controlling a process with real-time adjustments to plate polarity to replace temperature uniformity. In in other words, this research is essential for developers of plasma technology by providing a foundation for creating more effective devices with consistent results, such as plasma-enhanced chemical vapor deposition.

The proposed W-shaped network (WsNet) for automatic nucleus detection aims to enhance speed and precision simultaneously. To achieve this, the task is divided into two stages: nucleus classification and refined localization. In the initial stage, a lightweight classifier generates local interest maps, filtered to identify regions likely containing a nucleus. The subsequent localization stage employs a high-capacity parser to produce precise bounding boxes for the selected regions. We implement an attention mechanism in both stages to boost performance. Experimental results on two challenging datasets, NUTEC and WBC, demonstrate the superiority of WsNet over comparable models in terms of speed and accuracy.
