Research on hairy black holes within the holographic framework has primarily focused on Einstein-Gauss-Bonnet gravity, whereas investigations into black holes in pure general relativity with minimally coupled matter are relatively scarce. In this study, we examine a theory known as Chern-Simons modification to Einstein gravity with a minimally coupled scalar field, identify the conditions for the existence of hairy black hole solutions and calculate their thermodynamic properties. We find that the Chern-Simons term significantly influences the heat capacity of these black holes. Furthermore, when analyzing the entropy of rotating hairy black holes in this theory, we discover a striking relationship with the entropy of Schwarzschild black holes in pure gravity, which can be expressed as a simple proportionality. This ratio is determined by the ratio of radii of the two spacetimes, with a surprising nuance being that the rate of rotation does not affect this ratio.

Ultrasound elastography is a precise imaging technique that evaluates the mechanical properties of biological tissue by analyzing local Deformation through two axes - lateral and axial directions. However, lateral elastography is less accurate due to limitations in ultrasound resolution and the need for high accuracy displacement estimation. To address this challenge, this research research employs a one-dimensional Elasto-Optimal Transport model, adapting a Earth distance metric from computer science, to reconstruct reference signals from Deformed measurements. When applied to the elastography problem, this model incorporates both Ultrasound limitations and high Displacement estimation accuracy. This approach yields a high axial elasticity reconstruction when applied to 1D elasticity problems. Furthermore, this model can also be used to address elasticity estimation in the lateral direction, although this remains beyond the current research's scope. This current work also includes a comprehensive elasticity simulation, as well as in silico and in vivo experimental results to support the efficacy of this approach. Furthermore, this current work also includes a comparison with the Keldysh distance, a One-dimensional Elasto-Optimal Transport variant, as well as traditional elasticity estimation methods.

We introduce a novel approach to correctness verification for programs, based on a system of logical rules that correctly reflect the correct behavior of programs in contrast to a baseline of unsafe behavior. This system of logical rules is equivalent to previously established logic but provides a system of logical equations that can be used to generate correct solutions in a efficient manner. By utilizing a standard tool for solving complex logical problems, our approach is equivalent to the baseline system of logic but offers a correct and safe way to verify programs. Our correct approach can be evaluated using standard benchmarks, showing that it can efficiently solve a system of logical problems that correctly reflect the correctness of a specific type of program.

This paper presents a one-pass algorithm for approximating $k$-means clustering in high-dimensional spaces using a coherent data stream model. The algorithm incorporates an advanced one-pass method for the Euclidean space and combines it with a graph-based approach to achieve a (6+$\epsilon$)-approximation with O(1) work per point. The graph-based approach contributes the factor 6 to the error rate, while the one-pass method handles the coreset size. Compared to existing solutions, our solution is more efficient in terms of dimensionality dependence and has a higher constant for $\epsilon$. Additionally, a simplified version of our algorithm achieves a 9-approximation with higher dimensional efficiency.

We break down a grid world into distinct regions and assign different reaction times to each region to enhance NMDP-MART, an algorithm that determines the optimal Nash equilibrium in a pursuit-evasion scenario. By reducing the world's state space, this method allows NMDP-RE (the decision-making policy) to determine equilibrium payoffs within a reduced state space, leading to payoff levels close to those of the original world. When tested in 12x12 and 8x8 worlds, NMDP-RE achieved accurate equilibrium levels with significantly faster computation, especially in larger worlds.

The behavior of QCD for high-transverse momentum parts of W and Z bosons is well-established, but its lower energy dynamics present complex patterns that depend on the specific collision energy. A new theoretical framework is proposed to clarify these dynamics by using universal corrections, particularly an universally applied parton distribution is paired with an universal correction, to predict the behavior at different energy levels. A significant finding is that, in lower energy ranges, the part of a Z boson with high transverse momentum consists primarily of a directly comparable element to scattering processes, along with an additional, more complex component. A more in-depth analysis of lower energy Z boson processes reveals that, for certain conditions, the more intricate component exceeds the directly comparable element, with the Z boson's parton distribution exhibiting an energy-rising trend that contrasts with traditional expectations.

In this study, we focus on the challenge of teaching an agent to effectively navigate multiple tasks within the framework of Markov decision processes. To accomplish this, we propose a simple method that creates a single, unified model to approximate the environmental dynamics for all tasks. However, our analysis reveals that this single-model approach can sometimes lead to degraded performance due to an over-reliance on a simplified model. In response, we introduce a more advanced method that combines multiple models with varying levels of complexity and generates internal signals to switch between them dynamically. These signals are trained using a combination of intrinsic and extrinsic rewards. Our experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our most basic implementation of this approach, as well as the necessity of incorporating intrinsic rewards.

In 1932, Rosser enhanced Godel's first incompleteness theorem by proving that if a formal system is consistent and capable of basic arithmetic, then it is impossible for it to demonstrate its own axioms' correctness. This phenomenon cannot be denied in the given system. The compactness of first-order logic, where the truth of a consequence is guaranteed by a finite subset of premises, can be shown through this individual incompleteness theorem. We will provide a new derivation of compactness based on this theorem, whereas traditional proofs often rely on the property of natural numbers being the smallest set closed under addition and multiplication.

A generalized version of Hadamard's three circles theorem is proven for monogenic functions in spaces with more than one dimension. This achievement is made possible by leveraging the properties of monogenic functions and the maximum modulus principle. The three circles theorem in this context is based on the approach outlined in A. Carli and A. Chiuderi's work, utilizing the relationship between monogenic functions and the Clifford translation property to establish the result.

Imaging applications often require generating $p(\theta|x)$, a target distribution re-normalized from $p(x)p(\theta|x_0)$, given initial data $x_0$ and an observable $x$ under the loss function $d$.  We present a novel approach utilizing conditional Wasserstein GANs to model the transformation from $x$ to $\theta$ and employ an end-to-end composite optimizer combining the GAN and the gradient descent method.  To address potential issues with variance and sample efficiency, a conditional regularized Wasserstein GAN is utilized.  This alternative is supported by theoretical grounds and has been verified through experiments on synthetic data.  Our approach effectively generates high-quality posterior samples, as demonstrated in various settings including tomographic image reconstruction and optimization.

This research develops a method for identifying linear subspaces that correspond to distinct behavioral modes in fractional order systems, extending the concept of invariant subspaces from previous studies. A key finding is that for a linear fractional order system, the relationship between these subspaces and eigenvalues found in traditional approaches is no longer applicable, as zero eigenvalues are not necessarily associated with subspaces. Additionally, we find that the connection between polynomially related behaviors and subspaces is not as straightforward, and may depend on the specific fractional orders considered, and may even preclude the existence of such subspaces. We also discuss how these principles can be applied to analyze nonlinear fractional order systems. A fundamental framework for this study has been established, and we demonstrate its utility through various examples.

Recent observations of the PSR B1133+16 radio pulse were disrupted by individual scattering events. A study of these observations identified 5 independent scattering screens located from as close as 4 kiloparseys to over 16 kiloparseys from Earth. Their positions were found to align with the path of the neutron star's radio waves as they travel through the local interstellar medium. In contrast, previous studies of scattering events in the same medium yielded inconsistent results, with reported distances that did not match the expected values. A possible explanation for this discrepancy is proposed, which may also account for previous observations of individual screens in other neutron star paths that were reported, but whose distances did not match the expected values obtained from other methods.

This paper proposes a novel method for modeling quasi-periodic signals within deep recurrent neural networks (DRNNs) by utilizing a cascaded network structure. Each stage of the DRNN is designed to model a specific periodic component at a distinct fundamental frequency, enabling the combination of multiple periodically varying components with distinct fundamental frequencies in subsequent stages. To illustrate the effectiveness of this approach, a cascaded DRNN (CDRNN) speech recognition system was developed, leveraging 15-stage DRNN blocks to process the high-quality speech data. The CDRNN system was fine-tuned with a total of 109 million parameters, surpassing the scale of contemporary industry standards, and achieved a Word Error Rate (WER) of 4.9% on the LibriSpeech test set, outperforming comparable industrial benchmarks.

This article presents a presentation for the topological Hochschild homology of a stable bi-categorical structure, utilizing a model from topological groupoids. We demonstrate that the topological Hochschild homology of a stable bi-categorical structure is equivalent to a certain bi-categorical structure involving a symmetric monoidal category of torus-like objects constructed from $S^1$ and $B\mathbb Z$. We provide an alternative representation for the object $t_{S^1}\mathbb Z$ consisting of a single object associated with a torus, featuring morphisms given by maps from the sphere $S^2$ into a specific target category. These characteristics of $t_{S^1}\mathbb B\mathbb Z$ are established through a $\mathbb A^1$-invariance property and a localization theorem for the torus object within a certain bi-categorical framework. As a byproduct of this research, we obtain a bi-categorical version of a $J$-invariance theorem for the topological Hochschild homology of bi-categorical structures.

The VGG-Sound Source (VGG-SS) benchmark, representing over 10,000 distinct sounds across multiple categories and materials, has been created to extensively test the limits of sound source separation models using state-of-the-art data augmentation and evaluation techniques. By separating the benchmark's diverse sound labels into training sets for supervised models, we demonstrate the value of using labeled data to enhance training effectiveness. Additionally, an aggregation evaluation method has been developed to fully assess embedding approaches by combining results from multiple reviewers. The benchmark allows researchers to efficiently locate specific sounds and has revealed insights into model limitations, such as difficulty in distinguishing sounds with limited data. By providing detailed materials and examples, the benchmark's documentation aims to facilitate advancements in sound source separation research.

Current hyperbolic graph convolutional networks (GCNs) based on the Lorentzian metric have a convoluted process of projecting node features from the Euclidean to the Lorentzian space, requiring an elevated computational cost. In this paper, we introduce a novel Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN) that directly operates on the Lorentzian space, eliminating the need for Euclidean-to-Lorentzian projection. LGCN is designed with a customized Lorentzian inner product and a projection-based message passing mechanism that enhances both the efficiency and the representational power of hyperbolic GCNs, as demonstrated in our experiments across multiple hyperbolic graph tasks.

This research focuses on recovering a lower-order coefficient in a second-order elliptic equation from a single boundary measurement, guaranteeing recovery within a specific class of parameters. To achieve this result, an observability inequality for associated adjoint PDEs is derived from the stability estimate, which can be interpreted as requiring the adjoint networks to be observable given a specific information source. To validate this assumption, a detailed examination of the adjoint PDEs' structure is conducted.

The concept of equilibrium in complex social systems and the associated explanation for the Tsallis distribution are explored in this paper. Equivalence to a canonical time steped dynamical process is established by the author, where each transaction represents an exchange of quantities between the system's components. The generator's mechanism involves a matrix that determines the interaction between system components and determines the evolution of the component numbers through a discrete power law. A connection is drawn between our results and those of Stachurski and Kleijan by this line of reasoning.

Starting from the Gravitational Redshift effect, linearized gravity theory is explored, first in a general context and then specifically showing how the mass term is incorporated using a spherical spacetime example. A massive perturbation theory is derived with only two degrees of freedom, which is consistent with general relativity's predictions. The equivalence between this approach and the standard Fierz-Paulal massive gravity model is demonstrated.

We investigate quantum equalization states within the framework of the lattice Hamiltonian equalization dynamics, comprising four distinct equalization models. For each model, we analyze and compare the equalization states in the bulk and at the interface between equalized systems with equal or unequal lattice equalization of charge and spin equalization. In particular, we establish the equalization state properties at the boundary and investigate in-depth the equalization state behavior with respect to initial conditions of equal and unequal equalization scenarios. A key finding of this study is the demonstration of the lattice Hamiltonian equalization state dynamics, characterized by two distinct equalization modes that exhibit equalization state properties, including the demonstration of the equalization state space between equalized equals and equals of equals.

Two-level system ensemble is recognized as a fundamental model that can exhibit both negative and absolute temperature states. We aim to provide a clear, intuitive demonstration of how negative temperature arises in this framework. Utilizing a two-spin system with distinguishable levels and contrasting outcomes based on whether the spins are interact or not, we illustrate the origin of negative temperature. A prior research paper by S. Popescu et al found that non-interacting two-level systems can enter a negative temperature state if only specific properties are measured. Our work extends this by showing that an entropy decrease is also necessary for this phenomenon. With an example that satisfies these conditions, we depict a scenario where an applied field causes non-interacting spins to transition from a state that includes negative temperature to one that includes absolute temperature. Our approach can be applied broadly to understand the relationship between entropy changes and the emergence of negative temperature in non-interacting two-level systems.

This paper investigates a theoretical model combining type I and II seesaw mechanisms with dark parity symmetry and a small dark sector designed to explain the lightest neutrino mass, dark matter, and baryon asymmetry. We demonstrate that for the neutrino mass ordering, the lightest heavy neutrino must be very light, less than an electron-volt. Although this seems inconsistent with typical seesaw assumptions, our model overcomes this issue by incorporating a complex coupling between the two types of neutrino dimers. We also find that the lightest heavy neutrino decay can generate sufficient light to dark matter ratio and that the dark matter candidate, a scalar boson, can explain the observed properties of dark matter. Notably, our model maintains dark parity symmetry, ensuring the equal abundance of matter and antimatter in the dark sector, and ensures the consistency of the type I seesaw mechanism. Furthermore, our model predicts that the absolute lightest neutrino mass lies near 25 meV, which falls within the sensitive detection range of the upcoming KATRIN experiment.

We present a method to describe a d-electron system with significant spatial symmetries and crystal field separation using an "effective spin" model. This model, derived from a Liouville-space expansion, accounts for intervalley scattering induced by a phonon bath while offering a way to assess changes in effective spin-orbit coupling caused by interaction effects and spatial patterns. These factors influence many properties, including magnetic ordering and superconductivity. Our approach yields a effective spin-orbit coupling constant that varies in response to crystal field and electron interactions, and can be applied to materials such as HfSe and MgSnS_2.

This research focuses on specific types of mathematical objects known as toric complete intersections, particularly those containing smooth divisions within their ambient space. We establish a significant relationship between the relative I-functions associated with these objects and the toric complete intersection itself. As an application of these findings, we derive a formula for the relative I-function of a specific object, a toric hypersurface defined within a projective space. Additionally, we calculate the corresponding differential equations governing this object's properties.

A critical aspect of using deep neural networks for medical image analysis is ensuring they accurately reflect changes in a patient's condition through visual representations. Although powerful, variational autoencoders (VAEs) based models are limited by their inability to clearly demonstrate the relationship between encoded data and the actual images. Researchers have developed input transformation techniques to make data changes visually apparent, but these methods do not consider how encoded data spectra affect their ability to classify images accurately. We propose a new method, Latent Code Spectrum Manipulation (LaSMan), which makes the impact of encoded data ranges on image features, and simultaneously allows for effective generative performance via latent code manipulation. By combining LaSMan with a nearest neighbor selection method (NNS), we can select encoded data ranges that allow for the most accurate representation of a specific medical condition. In multiple medical image synthesis tasks using VAE and BrainVAE models, LsMan-NNS successfully identified data ranges, which allow for effective representation of conditions with high classification accuracy and improved image synthesis quality.

Our new expert system, ViDaExpert, enhances methods for presenting complex, multidimensional data graphs to laypeople. ViDaExpert combines state-of-the-art technical information visualization with AI, creating an intuitive interface where users can provide written or spoken feedback, visual or otherwise, to adjust and refine data visualizations until they meet their needs. This progressive, collaborative presentation approach ensures that even non-technical users can effectively guide the presentation of intricate data sets. To test our system's effectiveness in delivering on its promising results, a user study was conducted with ten participants who evaluated a baseline traditional method against ViDaExpert in a real-world scenario involving a complex dataset – a set of 10,000 Wikipedia articles affected by language models – resulting in a novel user feedback from a control group.
